The Labour Department announced today (the 10th) that Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) provided false information to the department during the local open recruitment period when applying to import foreign workers, and has been subject to administrative sanctions by the department, including immediately terminating the company's application and refusing to process the company's applications for the following year. Integrating the administrative sanction cases published by the Labour Department, FactWire has found that at least 18 companies have been penalised for violating regulations on importing foreign workers in the past, of which 10 companies are in the catering services and cleaning industries; among the 18 companies, 8 have been refused processing of foreign worker applications for one year by the Labour Department. Reporters have already inquired with the Labour Department for the latest figures on complaints, investigations, and administrative sanctions, and are still awaiting a reply.

Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) was subject to administrative sanctions by the Labour Department for providing false information during the local open recruitment period.

A spokesperson for the Labour Department stated that after investigation, it was confirmed that Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) provided false information during the local open recruitment period for importing waiters, junior chefs, and dishwashers, violating the regulations of the 'Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme', and was therefore imposed with administrative sanctions. The department has immediately terminated the company's submitted application for importing foreign workers, and refused to process the company's applications submitted under the Enhanced Scheme for the following year.

The department emphasised that employers importing foreign workers must strictly comply with the regulations of the scheme, including prioritising the employment of suitable local workers. If employers violate labour or immigration laws, the Enhanced Scheme, or the provisions of standard employment contracts, the Labour Department will impose administrative sanctions, including terminating the employer's submitted applications, revoking the employer's approved foreign worker quotas, and refusing to process applications subsequently submitted by the employer.

Reviewing Legislative Council data, since the launch of the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme in September 2023 and up to March this year, the Labour Department has received a total of 1,048 complaints, completed 287 complaint investigations; and imposed administrative sanctions on 35 employers for violating the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, occupational safety and health legislation, the Immigration Ordinance, or the regulations of the Enhanced Scheme.

Review of 18 Administrative Sanction Cases: Over Half Involve Catering and Cleaning Industries

The Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme was launched in September 2023, but amid a sluggish market and rising unemployment and underemployment rates, the government's continued importation of foreign workers has attracted concern. In August 2025, the authorities announced the first administrative sanction case, involving refusal of local jobseekers without reasonable grounds, immediately terminating the company's application and refusing foreign worker applications for the following year. In the same month later, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han stated that the foreign worker mechanism must not be abused, and that in the future, depending on the severity of the case and in response to public concern, the names of non-compliant employers would be disclosed where feasible.

FactWire has compiled the administrative sanction cases previously made public by the Labour Department. Including Waso Cafe (Prince Edward), which was sanctioned today, the Labour Department has imposed administrative sanctions on at least 18 employers for violating regulations on importing foreign workers, of which 6 companies are in the catering services industry and 4 are cleaning service companies; most of the sanctions were for refusing to employ local jobseekers without reasonable grounds, followed by providing false information. Among these, companies that refused to employ local workers were mostly refused foreign worker applications for the following two years, while some companies that provided false information were mostly suspended from processing for one year.

In two cases, Sheung Yuan Bistro Limited, which operates Sheung Yuan Chinese Restaurant, and Jantat Group Limited, which operates Yeng Yuen, were found to have dismissed local workers after employing foreign workers. They were refused applications for the following two years, and their previously approved foreign worker quotas were immediately revoked; however, the 11 foreign worker quotas already utilised by Sheung Yuan Chinese Restaurant may continue to remain employed in Hong Kong.

Reviewing Legislative Council data, the Labour Department previously stated that up to March this year, a total of 1,048 complaints had been received, with 287 complaint investigations completed; and administrative sanctions had been imposed on 35 employers for violating the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, occupational safety and health legislation, the Immigration Ordinance, or the regulations of the Enhanced Scheme. FactWire has already inquired with the Labour Department for the latest figures on complaints, investigations, and administrative sanctions, and is still awaiting a reply.
